light: This is one ordinary frame pulled from a normal handheld video shot by a ranch hand with a consumer camera at eye level, simply recording what happens, not composing a photo. The framing is casual and a little off: something is cut by the edge of the frame. Almost everything in the frame is in focus, nothing blurred out: the kitchen behind stays fully readable. The only light is what the place really has, and each person and object gets light according to where it stands; correctly exposed, daylight from the window and the open door, no lamps. Colours of an ordinary video with automatic white balance and almost no correction: moderate contrast, soft highlights, mild sensor noise and light compression, faint motion blur on anything moving. Skin with pores and uneven tone; hair with stray curls; the denim shirt faded and creased, the leather apron scuffed. Food looks like real home cooking, not styled. People are caught mid-action, unposed.
look: Ordinary handheld video filmed by a ranch hand with a consumer camera at eye level, small natural shakes and casual slightly imperfect framing, everything in the kitchen in focus, only the light the place really has, correctly exposed, automatic white balance, mild sensor noise; real skin and rough working hands; he moves naturally and unposed, nothing staged; no music.

clips.text: Now let me tell you why the old way fails, because it's not your fault. It's what everybody was taught. A dry bean is a seed. It's been dried until it's hard as a rock, so it'll keep for a year in a sack.
clips.action: Claudio, the man whose face is the third reference image, picks up one dry bean and holds it up between two fingers. daylight from the window and the open door, no lamps. He wears the same worn straw cowboy hat, faded blue denim snap shirt with rolled sleeves, red bandana and brown leather apron the whole time, same curly black-and-gray hair and short gray-black beard, same face as the reference.

clips.text: To cook it, you have to get water back inside it, all the way to the middle. That's what soaking is for. The skin softens, water soaks in slowly, and the bean swells back up.
clips.action: Claudio, the man whose face is the third reference image, drops the bean into a glass of water on the table. daylight from the window and the open door, no lamps. He wears the same worn straw cowboy hat, faded blue denim snap shirt with rolled sleeves, red bandana and brown leather apron the whole time, same curly black-and-gray hair and short gray-black beard, same face as the reference.

clips.text: The problem is, soaking all night is slow, and you have to remember to do it the night before. Most people don't. So the beans go in the pot hard,
clips.action: Claudio, the man whose face is the third reference image, taps his temple with a finger, 'you have to remember'. daylight from the window and the open door, no lamps. He wears the same worn straw cowboy hat, faded blue denim snap shirt with rolled sleeves, red bandana and brown leather apron the whole time, same curly black-and-gray hair and short gray-black beard, same face as the reference.

clips.text: and they boil and boil, and the outside cooks to mush while the middle is still chalky. And then people pour off the soaking water and salt at the end, because somebody told them salt makes beans tough.
clips.action: Claudio, the man whose face is the third reference image, mimes stirring a pot hard and fast, then stops. daylight from the window and the open door, no lamps. He wears the same worn straw cowboy hat, faded blue denim snap shirt with rolled sleeves, red bandana and brown leather apron the whole time, same curly black-and-gray hair and short gray-black beard, same face as the reference.

clips.text: That's not true. That's an old story. Cooks have tested it a hundred ways. Salt in the water at the start actually makes the skins softer, not harder, and it seasons the bean all the way to the middle.
clips.action: Claudio, the man whose face is the third reference image, shakes his head 'no' and holds up a pinch of salt between his fingers. daylight from the window and the open door, no lamps. He wears the same worn straw cowboy hat, faded blue denim snap shirt with rolled sleeves, red bandana and brown leather apron the whole time, same curly black-and-gray hair and short gray-black beard, same face as the reference.

clips.text: Salt at the end only sits on the outside. That's why your beans taste like nothing, and the broth tastes like salt. The last mistake is the big one. Boiling.
clips.action: Claudio, the man whose face is the third reference image, lets the salt fall back into a little salt dish and raises one finger. daylight from the window and the open door, no lamps.
